title: What is PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) — an extension for mobile/SPA apps that cannot safely store a client secret: generate a code_verifier + code_challenge, send challenge in auth request, send verifier in token exchange — prevents authorization code interception?
shortTitle: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) for Mobile and SPA Clients

s1_definition.profdef: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is an OAuth2 extension that secures the Authorization Code flow for public clients — mobile apps and single-page apps that cannot safely keep a client secret. The client generates a high-entropy random code_verifier, derives a code_challenge by hashing it (SHA-256), and sends only the challenge in the authorization request. When exchanging the code for a token, the client sends the original verifier; the Authorization Server hashes it and checks it matches the stored challenge. This proves the same client that started the flow is finishing it, so an intercepted authorization code is useless to an attacker who lacks the verifier.
s1_definition.analogy: A public app cannot keep a secret, so National Bank of India uses a one-time trick. When Rajesh starts logging in, his app invents a random secret phrase, keeps it hidden, and gives the bank only a sealed fingerprint of it (the hash). Later, to collect the access pass, the app must whisper the original phrase; the bank fingerprints the phrase on the spot and checks it matches the sealed fingerprint from the start. A thief who grabbed only the claim ticket cannot collect the pass because he never knew the secret phrase that produced the fingerprint.
s1_definition.oneliner: PKCE binds the code to a one-time secret only the real client knows, so a stolen code cannot be redeemed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is an OAuth2 extension that secures the Authorization Code flow for public clients — mobile apps and single-page apps that cannot safely keep a client secret. The client generates a high-entropy random code_verifier, derives a code_challenge by hashing it (SHA-256), and sends only the challenge in the authorization request. When exchanging the code for a token, the client sends the original verifier; the Authorization Server hashes it and checks it matches the stored challenge. This proves the same client that started the flow is finishing it, so an intercepted authorization code is useless to an attacker who lacks the verifier.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A public app cannot keep a secret, so National Bank of India uses a one-time trick. When Rajesh starts logging in, his app invents a random secret phrase, keeps it hidden, and gives the bank only a sealed fingerprint of it (the hash). Later, to collect the access pass, the app must whisper the original phrase; the bank fingerprints the phrase on the spot and checks it matches the sealed fingerprint from the start. A thief who grabbed only the claim ticket cannot collect the pass because he never knew the secret phrase that produced the fingerprint.

**One line to remember:** PKCE binds the code to a one-time secret only the real client knows, so a stolen code cannot be redeemed.

sections.s2_technical:
The client first creates a code_verifier, a random 43-to-128 character string, for example from 32 secure random bytes Base64Url-encoded. It then computes the code_challenge as `BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier))` and sends it in the authorize request with `code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256`. The Authorization Server stores the challenge against the issued code.

When the code comes back, the client exchanges it at the token endpoint and now includes the original verifier: `POST /token grant_type=authorization_code&code=...&code_verifier=...`. The server recomputes `SHA256(code_verifier)`, Base64Url-encodes it, and compares to the stored challenge. If they match, it issues the token; if not, it refuses. For example, an attacker who intercepted the code on a mobile device (via a malicious app registered on the same custom URL scheme) still cannot complete the exchange because they never had the verifier.

The senior nuances: PKCE replaces the client secret for public clients, and the S256 method should always be used over the weaker plain method, which sends the verifier as the challenge. Modern guidance recommends PKCE even for confidential clients as defense in depth, and the Implicit flow is deprecated in favor of Authorization Code plus PKCE for SPAs. PKCE specifically defeats authorization code interception; it does not replace the need for TLS, exact redirect_uri matching, or the state parameter for CSRF.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India mobile app is a public client: anyone can decompile it, so it cannot hold a client secret. Without a secret, a stolen authorization code could be redeemed by an attacker. This is exactly the gap PKCE fills — it supplies a per-request secret the attacker cannot know.

Problem 2 — On a phone, authorization codes come back via a custom URL scheme that a malicious app could also register and intercept. This is exactly the code interception attack PKCE defeats — the intercepted code is worthless without the matching verifier held only by the legitimate app.

Our mini-project builds a `PkceClient` that generates the verifier and challenge, and an `AuthorizationServer` that stores the challenge with the code and validates the verifier at exchange time. The demo shows a successful PKCE exchange and a failed exchange by an attacker who has the code but a wrong verifier.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a securely random code_verifier and the user rajesh.

Step 1: The PkceClient generates a 32-byte random verifier and derives the challenge as the Base64Url of SHA-256 over the verifier. The verifier stays secret on the device; only the challenge will be sent out.

Step 2: The authorize request carries only the challenge. The Authorization Server issues a code and stores the challenge alongside it. At this point the network only ever saw the hash, never the secret verifier.

Step 3: At token exchange the legitimate app sends the code plus the original verifier. The server recomputes SHA-256 of the verifier, compares to the stored challenge, finds a match, and issues the access token.

Step 4: An attacker who intercepted a code tries to exchange it but supplies a different verifier. The server hashes that verifier and gets a value that does not match the stored challenge, so it throws and refuses the token. The intercepted code is worthless without the one verifier that produced its challenge.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Mobile App (public client)              Authorization Server
      │ verifier = random (SECRET)             │
      │ challenge = SHA256(verifier) (PUBLIC)  │
      │  GET /authorize?code_challenge=CH&S256 │
      │───────────────────────────────────────▶ store CH with code
      │◀────────────── code ───────────────────│
      │  POST /token code + code_verifier=V    │
      │───────────────────────────────────────▶ SHA256(V) == CH ?
      │                                        │
      ├─ legit app: V matches CH ───────────▶ issue token
      └─ attacker: wrong V, SHA256 != CH ───▶ reject (code useless)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Authorization Code + PKCE (public clients) ═══

  ┌──────────────┐ challenge ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ Mobile / SPA │──────────▶│ Authorization Server│ bind challenge↔code
  │ (no secret)  │◀──code────│                     │
  └──────┬───────┘           └──────────┬──────────┘
         │ code + verifier              │ SHA256(verifier)==challenge?
         └──────────────────────────────┘ → token (or reject)
  No client_secret needed; verifier is the per-request proof
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — PKCE flow ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │        PkceClient        │        │   AuthorizationServer     │
  │ ──────────────────────── │        │ ───────────────────────── │
  │ + newCodeVerifier():Str  │        │ - codes: Map<code,        │
  │ + challengeFor(v):Str    │        │     {user, challenge}>    │
  │   (SHA256→base64url)     │        │ ───────────────────────── │
  └───────────┬──────────────┘        │ + issueCode(user,challenge)│
              │ verifier (secret)      │ + exchange(code,verifier) │
              │ challenge (public)────▶│   recompute, compare      │
              └───────────────────────▶└───────────────────────────┘

  Method contract exchange(code, verifier):
    Pre:  code exists & unused
    Post: token issued iff SHA256(verifier) == stored challenge
    Throws: PkceValidationException otherwise
  Always use S256 (never plain); PKCE defeats code interception
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
PKCE, Proof Key for Code Exchange, is an OAuth2 extension that secures the Authorization Code flow for public clients — mobile apps and single-page apps that cannot safely store a client secret. The client generates a random code_verifier, hashes it with SHA-256 to produce a code_challenge, and sends only the challenge in the authorization request. When it later exchanges the code for a token, it sends the original verifier, and the Authorization Server hashes it and checks it matches the stored challenge.

In my banking project the National Bank of India mobile app is a public client — it can be decompiled, so it cannot hold a secret. Without PKCE, an authorization code intercepted on the device, for example by a malicious app that registered the same custom URL scheme, could be redeemed by the attacker. PKCE closes that hole by binding the code to a one-time secret that only the legitimate app holds.

In my demo the app generates the verifier and challenge, the authorize request carries only the challenge, and the token exchange carries the verifier. The server re-hashes the verifier and confirms it matches, then issues the token. When an attacker presents a stolen code with the wrong verifier, the hash does not match the challenge and the server refuses, so the stolen code is useless.

The points I always add are that you should use the S256 method rather than the weaker plain method, that modern guidance recommends PKCE even for confidential clients as defense in depth, and that the old Implicit flow is deprecated in favor of Authorization Code plus PKCE for SPAs. PKCE specifically defeats code interception; it complements, and does not replace, TLS, exact redirect_uri matching, and the state parameter.

---

keyPoints: OAuth2: delegated authorization — app accesses user data on their behalf
Authorization Code Flow: safest for web apps — code exchanged server-to-server
PKCE: extra security for mobile/SPA — no client secret needed
OIDC: authentication layer on top of OAuth2 — ID token with user info
